topic: Notes on foundations: whether a question is decidable by finitely many operations, finiteness proofs with and without an upper bound, existence as consistency, and remarks on the spirit of mathematical research.

triage.modern_statement: This is not an open research problem. It is a standard example from the foundations of mathematics. The question 'what is the N-th decimal digit of π, for N = 10^(10^10)?' can be settled by a finite computation, so in principle it is decidable. In practice, though, it is far beyond any calculation anyone could actually do. Given the page's topic ('decidable by finitely many operations', finiteness proofs with or without a bound), Hilbert seems to be using it to separate 'decidable in principle' from 'feasibly decidable'. That distinction was argued over at the time, for example in Brouwer's critiques built on the digits of π.
triage.answered_by: Nobody has computed this digit, and current methods put it hopelessly out of reach. Related work: in 1995 the Bailey–Borwein–Plouffe (BBP) formula made it possible to compute the n-th digit of π directly, without the earlier digits, but only in hexadecimal (base 16). The largest full computation of π reached 314 trillion digits (about 3×10^14) in late 2025 (StorageReview, using y-cruncher). That is nowhere near position 10^(10^10), a number with ten billion digits.

evidence.claim: The BBP formula, discovered in 1995, computes a given hexadecimal digit of π without computing the digits before it.
The record computation of π reached 314 trillion digits in November 2025 (StorageReview, y-cruncher).

Questions about π's decimal expansion, such as whether 0123456789 ever occurs, were Brouwer's standard examples in his argument against the law of excluded middle. This is the foundational setting the note belongs to.
Constructive-mathematics explanations use digit patterns in π that have not yet been found to show what is at stake with excluded middle and finite decidability.

triage.why: The note is not one of Hilbert's 23 problems and it is not a known open problem. Any specific digit of π can be found by a finite computation, so in principle the question is settled. Read alongside the rest of the page, the line looks like a thought-experiment showing that 'decidable by finitely many operations' does not mean 'practically decidable'. It is not a request to actually find the digit. Digit-extraction algorithms and record computations are still active fields, but none of them comes close to position 10^(10^10). I found no source that discusses Hilbert's note itself, so the reading of his intent comes from the page context, not from a cited source.
